header.name: secret-redact-io
header.tagline: Read, write, fetch and run with the secrets stripped on the way out.

flows.title: What happens to a secret between the call and the caller
flows.footnote: The receipt is built from both texts and keeps neither. Its digests are over the bytes, not a copy of them.
flows.alt: Eight stages from call to return: call, raw bytes, policy, redact, persist, count, receipt, return. A call is one of four guarded operations: read a file, write a file, fetch a URL, run a program. The raw bytes come back from the file, the host or the process. The policy is a list of seven patterns applied in order. Each match is replaced by the name of the rule that matched it. On the write path the redacted text is what lands on disk, so the file is changed and not only the return value. The counts record how many times each rule fired. The receipt carries nine keys and none of them holds secret text. The caller receives the redacted text, which is the same text a write persisted. Three outcomes: redacted, untouched, and still leaking.

flows.title: Where a secret can still reach a receipt, and where it cannot
flows.footnote: A rule matches a shape. A credential that looks like ordinary prose has no shape to match, so it survives the pass.
flows.alt: Eight stages describing the honesty surface: rule list, shape, miss, target, metadata, query, argument, receipt. The policy is a fixed list of seven rules and nothing widens it at runtime. Each rule matches on shape, so a private key block, a key with a known prefix, or a value beside the word password is caught. A credential that reads as ordinary prose has no shape and passes through. The target field carries the name of the thing acted on rather than its content. Metadata is passed through exactly as the caller supplied it and no rule is applied to it. A fetch keeps only the scheme, host and path, so a token in a query string never reaches the receipt. An exec keeps only the base name of the program, so arguments never reach it either. The receipt is written from those fields plus two digests and the counts. Three outcomes: hash only, unmatched, and open field.

stages.title: Shape
stages.note: A rule matches form, never meaning.

stages.title: Miss
stages.note: A secret shaped like prose survives.

stages.title: Target
stages.note: The name of the thing, not its content.

stages.title: Metadata
stages.note: Passed through. No rule is applied.

stages.title: Query
stages.note: A fetch drops the query string whole.

stages.title: Argument
stages.note: An exec keeps the program name only.

stages.title: Receipt
stages.note: Two digests, the counts, four names.

returns.label: METADATA IS THE ONE FIELD NOTHING REDACTS

outcomes.label: HASH ONLY
outcomes.note: the receipt holds digests, not text

outcomes.label: UNMATCHED
outcomes.note: a secret the seven rules do not see

outcomes.label: OPEN FIELD
outcomes.note: metadata goes in exactly as given

cards.title: What a guardrail receipt records, and what it leaves out

fields.note: Stamped in UTC to the second when the receipt is built. Two runs over the same input differ here and nowhere else.
The raw bytes as they arrived, before any rule ran. It identifies the input without keeping any of it.
Whatever the caller passed, stored as given. No rule is applied to it, so this is the one field a secret can be written into.
Which path built this: read, write, write.dry_run, fetch, or exec.
How long the input was. A length, never the content behind it.
How long the returned text is. It moves away from raw_bytes when a replacement is a different length than what it replaced.
The returned text, digested. Running the same policy over the same input reproduces it.
Each rule that fired, and how many times. Rule names only, so a count of seven says nothing about what the seven were.
The file path, or the scheme, host and path of a URL, or the base name of a program. Arguments and query strings are dropped before this is set.

cards.alt: The nine keys a guardrail receipt returns, one to a row, each with what fills it. Two are digests, over the input bytes and over the returned text. Three are counts: the length of the input, the length of what came back, and how many times each rule fired. Two are names: which operation ran, and what it acted on, trimmed to a path or a program name. One is a clock stamp. The last is metadata, and its row is accented, because the caller fills it and nothing redacts what goes in.
cards.footnote: The receipt is built from the input and the redacted output together, which is how it can say how much changed without keeping what changed. Everything drawn here is either a hash, a count, or a name the tool trimmed itself. The exception is metadata, which is stored exactly as it was handed over.
